title: Research
text:
My research investigates how terrestrial and non-terrestrial communication networks can be designed, optimized, and operated more intelligently.
I work across multiple layers of the communication system—from mobility and radio-resource management to satellite-system planning and constellation design—using communication-system modeling, mathematical optimization, machine learning, algorithm development, and system-level simulation.
A recurring theme in my work is the interaction between three questions:

title: Research
text:
Research Areas

TN–NTN Mobility & Handover
How can seamless connectivity be maintained when users, networks, and satellite coverage are continuously changing?
The integration of terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks introduces mobility challenges that extend beyond conventional cellular handover. Satellite motion, evolving coverage, heterogeneous access networks, service requirements, and network availability all influence the mobility decision.
My research investigates mobility and handover mechanisms for integrated TN–NTN systems, ranging from demand-aware satellite handover to context-aware and AI/ML-assisted mobility management.
Current topics include:

TN–NTN mobility management
Satellite and beam handover
Context-aware and predictive handover
AI/ML-assisted mobility decisions
MNO–SNO cooperation
System-level mobility evaluation

Explore my research perspective on TN–NTN handover →



Radio Resource Management & Optimization
How should limited communication resources adapt to changing traffic, interference, and network conditions?
A major theme throughout my research is the efficient management of communication-system resources.
I have worked on problems involving power, bandwidth, beams, traffic demand, interference, scheduling, and payload resources, particularly in multi-beam and flexible satellite communication systems.
My work combines mathematical optimization with heuristic, combinatorial, and learning-assisted approaches to develop resource-management strategies that respond to heterogeneous traffic demand and operational constraints.
Key topics include:

Power and bandwidth allocation
Demand-aware resource management
Interference-aware optimization
Scheduling and link adaptation
Beam and payload-resource management
Flexible satellite systems
Onboard processing-resource management




Beamforming, Precoding & Beam Management
How can spatial resources be used more effectively to improve capacity and manage interference?
My research background includes physical-layer and system-level techniques for improving spectral efficiency and managing interference in wireless and satellite communication systems.
This includes work on precoding, beamforming, beam management, interference mitigation, and multi-beam communication systems, particularly where physical-layer techniques interact with resource-allocation and system-level decisions.
I am especially interested in problems where beam design cannot be treated independently from traffic demand, resource availability, interference, and network geometry.



Beam Placement & Resource Allocation
Where should satellite beams be placed, and how should resources be assigned to them under non-uniform traffic demand?
My work also considers the joint design of beam placement and radio-resource allocation, particularly for large-scale MEO satellite systems.
These problems connect coverage decisions with the allocation of bandwidth, power, and satellite resources, while accounting for traffic demand, satellite visibility, payload limitations, and interference.
This research provides a bridge between dynamic resource management and the broader problem of satellite-network planning.
View related publications →



Satellite System Planning & Constellation Optimization
What satellite capabilities—and what constellation architecture—are required to deliver a target communication service?
My research increasingly addresses decisions that arise before a satellite network is deployed.
At the satellite level, I investigate how communication and service requirements can be translated into appropriate system resources and satellite capabilities.
At the network level, I study how constellation characteristics can be optimized according to coverage, communication, visibility, and service requirements.
Current topics include:

Satellite resource planning
System dimensioning
Constellation optimization
Orbital and coverage analysis
Satellite visibility
Communication-aware constellation design
6G satellite connectivity
Direct-to-Device connectivity

Explore my research perspective on satellite planning and constellation optimization →



AI/ML for Communication Networks
Where can learning provide a measurable advantage over model-based optimization and conventional network algorithms?
I investigate machine-learning approaches for communication-system problems involving mobility, handover, resource management, network planning, and sequential decision making.
My interest is not in applying AI/ML independently of the communication problem. Instead, I am interested in combining learning with physical models, system constraints, domain knowledge, and mathematical optimization.
This includes research directions such as:

Reinforcement learning for mobility and handover
Learning-assisted resource management
Prediction and context-aware network decisions
Hybrid optimization and learning
Learning-assisted system planning

title: Research
text:
Connecting the Research Areas
Although these topics can be studied independently, many of the most interesting problems emerge from their interaction.
For example:
Mobility ↔︎ Resource Management
A handover decision affects network load and resource availability, while available resources can influence whether a handover is beneficial.
Resource Management ↔︎ System Planning
Operational resource-allocation problems depend on the capabilities designed into the satellite and payload.
System Planning ↔︎ Constellation Design
Satellite capabilities influence the number and configuration of satellites required to provide a target service.
Constellation Design ↔︎ Mobility
Altitude, satellite density, visibility duration, and coverage overlap influence handover frequency and service continuity.
AI/ML ↔︎ Optimization
Learning can complement model-based approaches when decisions involve prediction, uncertainty, complex dynamics, or large design spaces.
These connections motivate a broader system-level perspective rather than treating mobility, resource management, and network design as completely separate problems.

title: Research
text:
Research Evolution
My research has progressively moved across different levels of satellite and wireless communication-system design.

Flexible Satellite Resource Management
My doctoral research at the University of Luxembourg focused on resource-management techniques for flexible broadband satellite communication systems.
The work investigated the efficient use of power, bandwidth, beams, and payload resources under heterogeneous traffic demand and interference conditions.
Research topics included:

Flexible resource optimization
Power and bandwidth allocation
Demand-aware resource management
Interference-aware resource management
Flexible payload-resource management
Onboard processing-resource management

This work established the resource-optimization foundation that continues to influence my current research.


5G Algorithm & System-Level Simulation
My industrial R&D experience at Nokia extended this perspective to terrestrial cellular systems.
As a Senior Algorithm and Simulation Engineer, I worked on algorithm development, performance evaluation, and system-level simulation for 5G systems, providing experience with 3GPP-based cellular-system development and industrial simulation methodology.


Integrated TN–NTN & Satellite Network Design
My current research extends these foundations toward broader questions involving TN–NTN mobility, intelligent handover, satellite-system planning, constellation optimization, Direct-to-Device connectivity, and AI/ML-assisted network decision making.
This progression connects operational questions—such as how resources should be allocated—with architectural questions about what resources should exist and how future terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks should be designed.

title: Research
text:
Research Methodology
My research combines several complementary approaches.
Communication-System Modeling
Link budgets, channel models, traffic modeling, scenario definition, orbital and coverage analysis, and system-level abstraction.
Mathematical Optimization
Continuous, discrete, combinatorial, heuristic, and metaheuristic approaches for communication-system design and resource management.
Machine Learning
Learning-assisted and reinforcement-learning approaches for mobility, resource management, prediction, and network decision making.
Algorithm Development
Translation of mathematical and system models into practical algorithms suitable for performance evaluation.
System-Level Simulation
Implementation, comparative evaluation, sensitivity analysis, and performance assessment under representative communication scenarios.

title: Tedros Salih Abdu
text:
I am a researcher at the Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust (SnT), University of Luxembourg, working on the design and optimization of next-generation wireless communication systems.
My research focuses on terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks (TN/NTN), particularly mobility and handover, radio-resource management, satellite system planning and constellation optimization, and the application of mathematical optimization and machine learning to communication networks.
My background combines academic research, industrial R&D, and research-project leadership.
Research Publications Google Scholar









My research addresses a central challenge in future wireless networks:

How can increasingly dynamic terrestrial and non-terrestrial communication systems make better decisions about connectivity, resources, and network architecture?

I approach this challenge across four interconnected dimensions:



Enabling seamless mobility and handover across terrestrial cells, satellite beams, and moving satellite networks.



Developing methods to allocate power, bandwidth, beams, and network resources efficiently under changing traffic and system conditions.



Connecting service requirements with satellite-system planning and constellation design for future 6G and Direct-to-Device connectivity.



Investigating where machine learning can complement mathematical optimization for mobility, resource management, and network decision making.








How can users move seamlessly between terrestrial networks, satellite beams, and moving satellites?
I study mobility and handover in integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks, including demand-aware satellite handover, MNO–SNO cooperation, context-aware mobility, and AI/ML-assisted handover decisions.
Explore TN–NTN mobility research →




How should limited communication resources adapt to changing traffic, interference, and network conditions?
My work investigates the efficient management of power, bandwidth, beams, scheduling, interference, and payload resources across GEO, MEO, and NGSO satellite communication systems.
I use mathematical optimization together with heuristic and learning-assisted approaches to develop resource-management strategies that adapt to heterogeneous traffic demand and system constraints.




What satellite capabilities—and what constellation architecture—are needed to deliver a target communication service?
I investigate the connection between service requirements, satellite resource planning, system dimensioning, orbital characteristics, coverage, and constellation optimization.
This research moves beyond operating an existing satellite system toward determining what resources and network architecture should be deployed in the first place.
Explore satellite planning research →




Where can learning provide a measurable advantage over conventional optimization and rule-based methods?
I investigate machine-learning approaches for mobility management, handover, resource optimization, network planning, and intelligent decision making.
Rather than treating AI as an objective by itself, I am interested in understanding where learning can complement communication-system models and mathematical optimization to improve network performance and adaptability.







One of my current research directions is the development of intelligent mobility and handover mechanisms for integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks.
Future users may move—or maintain connectivity—across terrestrial cells, satellite beams, and different satellites. This makes mobility management a decision problem involving not only radio conditions, but also satellite visibility, network availability, user requirements, resources, and expected service continuity.
I currently serve as VPI of SHINE, where my work focuses on intelligent mobility and handover for integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks.
My activities include research and technical leadership, system and scenario modeling, development of technical specifications, technical baseline definition, coordination of technical activities, reporting, and dissemination.

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
text:
The integration of terrestrial networks (TN) and non-terrestrial networks (NTN) creates new opportunities for ubiquitous and resilient connectivity. It also changes the nature of mobility management.
In a conventional terrestrial network, handover is primarily associated with user movement between cells. In NTN, the network itself may be moving: satellites and their coverage areas evolve continuously relative to users on the ground.
When TN and NTN are integrated, mobility management therefore becomes a broader decision problem involving radio conditions, satellite visibility, user demand, network availability, service requirements, and handover cost.
My research in this area has evolved from demand-aware handover in LEO constellations toward intelligent mobility management for integrated TN–NTN systems.

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
section: From LEO Handover to TN–NTN Mobility
text:
From LEO Handover to TN–NTN Mobility
LEO constellations introduce an inherent mobility challenge. Even for a stationary user, the serving satellite remains visible only for a limited period.
This leads to a fundamental question:

How can continuous service be maintained while avoiding unnecessary handovers?

In our earlier work on demand-aware flexible handover for LEO constellations, we considered handover together with user traffic demand. The objective was to reduce the number of handovers while continuously satisfying the required user demand.
This work motivated a broader perspective: handover should not depend only on which satellite is visible or which link is strongest. The decision should also consider whether the serving network can continue satisfying the user’s service requirements.
The problem becomes more complex in integrated TN–NTN systems because a user may have multiple connectivity alternatives, including terrestrial cells, satellite beams, and different satellites.
The decision therefore changes from:

Which satellite should serve the user?

to:

Which network, cell, beam, or satellite should serve the user, and when is switching actually beneficial?

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
section: Handover Is More Than a Radio Decision
text:
Handover Is More Than a Radio Decision
Integrated TN–NTN mobility involves several interacting factors:

radio-link quality,
satellite visibility and coverage evolution,
terrestrial-network availability,
user mobility,
traffic and service requirements,
network load,
handover interruption,
connection failures,
and ping-pong behavior.

There is also an architectural dimension.
Terrestrial connectivity may be provided by a Mobile Network Operator (MNO) while satellite connectivity is provided by a Satellite Network Operator (SNO).
Our work on MNO–SNO cooperation examined how roaming and network cooperation affect mobility between terrestrial and satellite networks. This highlights an important point: seamless TN–NTN mobility depends not only on the handover algorithm but also on the architecture supporting the transition.
Future handover mechanisms may therefore need to reason jointly about radio conditions and network context.

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
text:
From Rule-Based to Intelligent Handover
Conventional handover mechanisms commonly use radio measurements together with parameters such as thresholds, hysteresis, and time-to-trigger.
These mechanisms remain important, but integrated TN–NTN environments introduce additional information that could potentially improve mobility decisions.
For example, a handover controller could consider:
Radio context — signal quality, interference, and link availability.
NTN context — satellite position, elevation, visibility duration, and beam evolution.
User context — mobility, traffic demand, and service requirements.
Network context — load, resource availability, and candidate-network conditions.
Architectural context — MNO/SNO cooperation and expected handover interruption.
Predictive context — future satellite visibility and expected network conditions.
This changes handover from a largely reactive event toward a potentially context-aware and predictive decision process.

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
text:
Learning-Based Mobility Management
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) provides one framework for studying such sequential mobility decisions.
Instead of optimizing each handover independently, an RL agent can learn a policy that considers the longer-term consequences of remaining with the current network or moving to another candidate.
In our recent work, we evaluated PPO, A2C, and DQN for handover management across hybrid TN–NTN scenarios.
An important observation is that the relative behavior of these algorithms depends on the considered coverage environment. This suggests that simply introducing AI/ML does not automatically solve the mobility problem.
The state representation, reward formulation, network scenario, training environment, and algorithm all matter.
For me, this leads to a more interesting research question:

How can mobility intelligence adapt to the characteristics of the TN–NTN environment rather than relying on one fixed handover strategy?

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
text:
Research Directions
Building on these results, I am particularly interested in four directions.

1. Context-Aware and Predictive Handover
Satellite trajectories provide information that is fundamentally different from conventional terrestrial mobility: much of the satellite motion is predictable.
This creates opportunities to combine current radio measurements with information about:

future satellite visibility,
expected coverage evolution,
user trajectory,
service requirements,
and network conditions.

A key question is whether this information can enable proactive handover decisions rather than waiting until link degradation triggers a transition.



2. Hybrid Optimization and Learning
My earlier LEO handover work used optimization-based methods, while more recent work investigates learning-based mobility management.
These approaches have complementary strengths.
Model-based optimization can exploit known system structure and constraints. Learning can be useful when decisions involve complex dynamics and long-term consequences.
This motivates hybrid approaches such as:

optimization-guided reinforcement learning,
learning-assisted candidate selection,
model-based constraints for learned policies,
and hierarchical TN–NTN decision making.

The objective is not simply to replace optimization with AI, but to determine where learning adds measurable value.



3. Service- and Resource-Aware Mobility
The strongest instantaneous radio link may not always be the most appropriate serving network.
Future mobility decisions could jointly consider:

link quality,
user QoS,
traffic demand,
terrestrial and satellite resources,
network congestion,
and expected connection duration.

This connects mobility management with another major area of my research: radio-resource management.
A broader question is therefore:

Can mobility and resource management be optimized jointly rather than treated as independent network functions?




4. Mobility-Aware TN–NTN Architecture
The network architecture itself can influence handover latency, signaling, and service continuity.
This makes MNO–SNO cooperation, core-network integration, and mobility procedures part of the research problem.
An important direction is to investigate which architectural assumptions enable intelligent mobility mechanisms to operate effectively and how mobility algorithms should adapt when those assumptions change.

title: Rethinking Handover for Integrated TN–NTN Networks
text:
Research Perspective
The evolution from LEO satellite handover toward integrated TN–NTN mobility suggests that future handover mechanisms will need to operate across several dimensions:
radio conditions + satellite dynamics + user requirements + network resources + architecture + prediction
The research challenge is therefore broader than finding a better handover threshold.
The objective is to determine when to hand over, where to hand over, and whether a handover is worthwhile, while maintaining service continuity and using terrestrial and non-terrestrial resources efficiently.
This is the direction I am continuing to explore through system modeling, mathematical optimization, machine learning, and system-level evaluation.

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
text:
Designing a satellite network involves decisions at multiple levels.
At the satellite level, we need to determine what communication and payload capabilities are required. At the network level, we need to determine how many satellites are needed, how they should be deployed, and whether the resulting constellation can satisfy the intended service requirements.
My recent research approaches these questions from two connected directions: satellite resource planning and constellation optimization.
Together, they motivate a broader question:

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
section: From Resource Allocation to Resource Planning
text:
From Resource Allocation to Resource Planning
Much of satellite resource management starts with an existing system and asks how available resources should be allocated.
Typical decisions involve:

power,
bandwidth,
beams,
payload resources,
and traffic demand.

Resource planning asks an earlier question:

What resources should the satellite system have before it is deployed?

This distinction is important because service requirements influence not only how resources are allocated, but potentially the physical and system-level characteristics of the satellite.
In our work on resource planning for next-generation satellite communication systems, we investigated how communication requirements can be translated into candidate satellite-system specifications.
The planning framework considers parameters associated with:

spot beams,
DC power,
antenna dimensions,
satellite mass,
and system cost.

This creates a connection between communication-system requirements and satellite-system design.

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
section: From Satellite Planning to Constellation Design
text:
From Satellite Planning to Constellation Design
For a non-geostationary satellite network, designing an individual satellite is only part of the problem.
Network performance also depends on the constellation architecture, including:

orbital altitude,
number of satellites,
orbital geometry,
coverage,
satellite visibility,
and communication-link requirements.

This leads to a second question:

Given the capabilities of the satellites, what constellation is required to deliver the target service?

Our recent work on satellite constellation optimization for 6G and beyond investigates this problem in the context of connectivity to handheld devices.
The formulation considers communication and visibility requirements together with orbital characteristics and seeks to determine a constellation satisfying the considered requirements with a reduced number of satellites.
This connects orbital design with communication-system performance.

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
section: Coverage Is Not the Same as Service
text:
Coverage Is Not the Same as Service
An important distinction in satellite-network planning is between geometric coverage and service availability.
A satellite may be visible to a user without necessarily providing a communication link capable of satisfying the target service.
This distinction becomes particularly important for Direct-to-Device (D2D) connectivity, where handheld-terminal capabilities impose challenging link-budget constraints.
For future constellation design, the relevant question is therefore not simply:

Is a satellite visible?

but:

Can a visible satellite provide the required service?

This motivates a more service-aware approach to constellation planning.

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
text:
The Constellation Design Trade-Off
Orbital altitude illustrates the interaction between constellation architecture and communication performance.
Lower-altitude satellites benefit from shorter communication distances, but an individual satellite covers a smaller geographic region and a larger constellation may therefore be required.
At higher altitudes, individual satellites can cover larger regions, but the longer communication distance makes the link budget more demanding.
This creates a coupled design problem involving:
altitude ↔︎ constellation size ↔︎ satellite capability ↔︎ communication performance
Studying these quantities jointly is more informative than optimizing any one of them in isolation.

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
text:
Research Directions
Building on the two studies, I am particularly interested in four broader directions.

1. Joint Resource and Constellation Optimization
Satellite resource planning and constellation optimization are naturally connected.
Instead of designing satellite capabilities first and determining constellation size afterward, a future framework could optimize them jointly.
For example, there may be a trade-off between deploying:

more satellites with relatively modest capabilities, or
fewer satellites with greater communication and payload capabilities.

A joint formulation could expose trade-offs involving satellite count, mass, power, antenna characteristics, capacity, and cost.
The central question is:

What combination of satellite capability and constellation architecture provides the required service most efficiently?




2. Traffic- and Service-Aware Constellation Planning
Global communication demand is highly non-uniform.
Population distribution, transportation corridors, maritime and aviation traffic, and terrestrial-network availability all affect where satellite capacity is actually required.
This suggests moving beyond uniform geographic coverage toward traffic-aware and service-aware planning.
A possible design chain is:
traffic demand → service requirements → satellite resources → constellation architecture
This could also incorporate different requirements for broadband, IoT, emergency connectivity, or Direct-to-Device services.



3. Mobility-Aware TN–NTN Constellation Design
Constellation architecture determines more than coverage.
Satellite density, altitude, coverage overlap, and visibility duration also influence:

handover frequency,
candidate-satellite availability,
connection duration,
and mobility robustness.

This creates a direct connection with my research on TN–NTN mobility and handover.
A future constellation could therefore be designed not only for coverage and capacity, but also for efficient mobility.
In an integrated TN–NTN system, terrestrial coverage could also become part of the planning problem:

Where and when does NTN actually need to provide coverage or additional capacity given the capabilities of the terrestrial network?

This connects satellite planning with the broader architecture of future integrated networks.



4. Adaptive and Learning-Assisted Planning
Satellite systems operate for many years, while traffic demand and service requirements can evolve significantly.
Planning solely for one expected operating condition may therefore result in an architecture that becomes inefficient as demand changes.
Future approaches could incorporate:

uncertainty in traffic demand,
flexible or software-defined payload capabilities,
robust and scenario-based optimization,
multi-objective optimization,
and learning-assisted search.

AI/ML may be particularly useful for accelerating large design-space exploration or learning surrogate models for expensive system evaluations.
However, I see learning as a complement to, rather than an automatic replacement for, mathematical and model-based optimization.
The key question is:

Where can learning provide a measurable advantage while preserving the physical structure and constraints of the satellite-system problem?

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
text:
A Broader Research Framework
These directions suggest a broader view of satellite-network design:
Service Requirements
↓
Traffic & Coverage Modeling
↓
Satellite Resource Planning
↓
Constellation Optimization
↓
Dynamic Resource & Mobility Management
The interesting research opportunity is that these stages do not necessarily need to be independent.
Mobility requirements could influence constellation design. Terrestrial coverage could influence required satellite capacity. Payload flexibility could influence how aggressively a system must be optimized before deployment.
This creates the possibility of moving from individual optimization problems toward system-level co-design.

title: From Satellite Resource Planning to Constellation Optimization
text:
Research Perspective
My earlier work focused primarily on managing resources within satellite systems. These more recent studies move the question progressively toward planning what resources should exist and what network architecture should provide them.
The broader question therefore becomes:

What satellite resources should be deployed, what constellation architecture should provide them, and how should those resources subsequently be managed?

I see three connected levels:
Design — what system should be built?
Planning — what resources and architecture are required to support the intended services?
Operation — how should those resources be dynamically managed after deployment?
Connecting these levels is an interesting direction toward satellite networks that are more service-aware, resource-efficient, flexible, and responsive to changing demand.

title: About
text:
I am Tedros Salih Abdu, a researcher at the Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust (SnT), University of Luxembourg. My work focuses on the design and optimization of next-generation wireless communication systems, particularly terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks.
My background spans academic research, industrial R&D, and collaborative research-project leadership, with experience in mathematical optimization, machine learning, algorithm development, and system-level simulation for wireless and satellite communication systems.

title: About
text:
Background
I received my Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Luxembourg in 2022, where my doctoral research focused on resource-management techniques for flexible broadband satellite communication systems.
I received a joint M.Sc. degree in Electrical Engineering from Pan African University and Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Kenya, in 2017, and a B.Sc. degree in Electronics and Communication Engineering from Mekelle University.
My professional experience spans both academia and industry. From 2017 to 2019, I was a Lecturer at Wollo University. I subsequently joined the University of Luxembourg, where I worked as a Doctoral Researcher and later as a Research Associate.
I also worked at Nokia as a Senior Algorithm and Simulation Engineer, contributing to algorithm development and system-level simulation for 5G systems. I later returned to SnT, University of Luxembourg, where I currently work on research and development for next-generation terrestrial and non-terrestrial communication systems.

title: Roaming or Handover for Integrated TN–NTN?
text:
Integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks require users to move between the coverage of Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) and Satellite Network Operators (SNOs).
This raises an important mobility question:
Our recent work investigates this question by comparing different MNO–SNO cooperation mechanisms for integrated TN–NTN networks.

title: Roaming or Handover for Integrated TN–NTN?
text:
Roaming or Handover?
Traditionally, mobility within the coverage of the same operator is handled through handover, while movement from a Home Public Land Mobile Network (HPLMN) to another operator’s network is handled through roaming.
In an integrated TN–NTN system, however, a user may need to switch from an MNO to an SNO when terrestrial coverage becomes limited or unavailable.
Conventional roaming can introduce significant service interruption because the UE may lose its connection with the home network before searching for and connecting to the visited network.
This becomes particularly important for high-mobility users, such as users travelling on high-speed trains.

title: Roaming or Handover for Integrated TN–NTN?
text:
Mobility Mechanisms for MNO–SNO Transitions
Existing approaches for mobility between terrestrial and satellite networks include mechanisms such as Release-with-Redirect, inter-PLMN handover, and RACH-less handover. These mechanisms and their associated signaling procedures are reviewed in our previous work.
See the discussion in our paper
Rather than revisiting these mechanisms individually, an interesting research question is:

When should a transition between an MNO and an SNO be handled as roaming, and when should it be handled as a coordinated handover?

This question becomes particularly relevant when terrestrial and satellite connectivity are not isolated alternatives, but complementary parts of an integrated network through which a user may transition repeatedly.

title: Roaming or Handover for Integrated TN–NTN?
text:
ML-Assisted Handover
Another challenge is deciding whether the UE should hand over to another terrestrial cell or switch to the satellite network.
Our work proposes an ML-assisted Conditional Handover (CHO) approach.
The candidate terrestrial cell is first selected based on Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP). An ML model then predicts the future elevation angle of the moving UE relative to the candidate terrestrial gNB.
The prediction helps determine whether the terrestrial target remains appropriate as the UE continues moving. Otherwise, the UE can switch to—or remain connected with—the satellite network.
The objective is to reduce mobility problems such as connection failures and ping-pong events, while improving the success of MNO–SNO cooperation.

title: Roaming or Handover for Integrated TN–NTN?
text:
Research Perspective
The results raise an interesting question for integrated TN–NTN mobility:

When should an MNO–SNO transition rely on roaming, and when should it be handled through inter-PLMN handover?

Roaming provides an established mechanism for mobility between different operators, but its interruption time can be problematic when seamless connectivity is required.
Inter-PLMN handover, particularly when combined with mechanisms such as RACH-less access and ML-assisted mobility decisions, provides another direction for supporting transitions between terrestrial and satellite networks.
This suggests that the design of future TN–NTN mobility should consider not only which network the UE should connect to, but also which mobility procedure should be used to perform the transition.
